notes.chapter: Cap. 17: Como una autopista: encuentros de electrónica y música popular (1989-2002)
notes.text: «La culpa la tuvo el éxtasis»: tras el pop en claroscuro (Joy Division, The Smiths) y la Inglaterra de Thatcher, del magisterio de The Haçienda surge una generación de rock con amor por el dance. The Stone Roses (debut de 1989) y Happy Mondays (Pills ’n’ Thrills and Bellyaches, producido por Paul Oakenfold) actúan juntos en Top of the Pops el 23 de noviembre de 1989, «el auténtico comienzo de los noventa». Ropa baggy, camisetas («Y en el séptimo día, Dios creó Manchester») y el himno mundialista «World in Motion». En 1992 el declive hunde Factory. Fuera de Manchester: Jesus Jones, EMF, The Farm, The Soup Dragons, World of Twist.

refs.para: Balearic, precisamente, fue un término del que se abusó en exceso, primero por desorientación y más tarde por exigencias del márketing. En el principio balearic podía aplicarse desde cualquier atisbo de música inspirada por un verano en Ibiza, desde los primeros éxitos del acid inglés, ya fueran los de D-Mob («We Cali It Acieed») o E-Zee Posse («Everything Starts with an E») o el gigantesco crossover hacia el pop que logró Adamski con «Killer», un hit inmenso en la voz de Seal y un videoclip, entre Kraftwerk y David Cronenberg, que daba a entender, por toda su imaginería apocalíptica y sci-fi, que las cosas estaban cambiando. Andrew Weatherall, por su parte, empezó con Pete Heller y Terry Farley un proyecto fugaz (sus respectivas carreras, como productores y DJ, les ocuparon el tiempo suficiente como para que la cosa no continuara más allá de 1990) que, llamado Bocea Juniors, facturó una pieza canónica, «Raise (63 Steps to Heaven)»: riffs de piano, trompetas funk, acid rebotado en rock y un punto new wave. De hecho, música de baile y rock se contaminaban ya recíprocamente, y el muy singular fenómeno Madchester —grupos de pop en Manchester aplicando loops electrónicos, efectos, beats de house y baile en escena— empezaba a demostrar también que no había vuelta atrás ni siquiera para la clásica formación de voz-guitarra-bajo-batería. Cuando el propio Weatherall se encargó de la producción del totémico Screamadelica (Primal Scream), el cambio ya era un hecho.

refs.q: La culpa la tuvo el éxtasis
refs.para: La culpa la tuvo el éxtasis. Después de años de pop en claroscuro Joy Division, The Smiths), de clubes elitistas donde importaba más tu aspecto que tu música favorita y de un gobierno, el de Margaret Thatcher, cuyo objetivo prioritario era el fin de la comunidad («no existe la sociedad, solo existen los individuos», sentenció la Dama de Hierro), la llegada de la nueva droga (y de su son: el acid house) supuso una bendición para la juventud de Manchester. Del magisterio del The Hacienda surgió una generación de bandas rock con amor por los procederes dance, una generación que tenía ante sí la opción de superar un pasado mediocre. Héroes del pop de todos los tiempos, Happy Mondays y The Stone Roses han quedado como las cabezas mejor amuebladas de una escena que, prolongando la corriente avant-funk de Quando Quango, fortaleció de modo espectacular y del todo trascendente el entendimiento entre las estructuras del rock y de la música de baile. Right on, right on.
refs.chapter: Cap. 17: Como una autopista: encuentros de electrónica y música popular (1989-2002)

refs.q: en lo que algunos consideran el auténtico comienzo de los noventa
refs.para: El 23 de noviembre de 1989, The Stone Roses y Happy Mondays hicieron juntos su primer Top of the Pops gracias a «Fool’s Gold» y «Hallelujah», respectivamente, en lo que algunos consideran el auténtico comienzo de los noventa. «Hallelujah» era el corte principal del Madchester Rave on EP, que renombró a Manchester por razones consistentes: la ciudad agitaba el tejido musical moderno, se abría veinticuatro horas a la fiesta y era espacio abierto a la comunión de ideologías. Y es que «Madchester» supuso toda una escena, con sus propias bandas (a las ya mentadas, sumen The Charlatans, Inspiral Carpets, Northside o Paris Angels), su propia ropa (baggy, esto es, «que hace bolsas»), sus propios clubes y sus propios lemas: «Y en el séptimo día, Dios creo Manchester», «Woodstock ‘69, Manchester ‘89», «Esto no es Manchester, esto es un trip» o los de la serie «Cool As Fuck»; sentencias impresas sobre camisetas que vistieron hooligans de Manchester y Londres, Liverpool y Leeds, hermanados por la droga, la música, la necesidad de una escapada.

own_scenes.desc: En 1988, fuera del círculo de Rhythm King, había que ir a Mánchester para oír discos de Detroit: en la Haçienda (financiada por New Order) Mike Pickering, criado en el soul, pinchaba «Goodbye Kiss», «Groovin’ without a Doubt» o «Triangle of Love» antes que nadie en Londres, donde en el Spectrum no sonaban. La ciudad de los Smiths, The Fall y New Order unió el indie al acid house con los Happy Mondays, los Stone Roses e Inspiral Carpets, un puente hacia 808 State y A Guy Called Gerald.

influences.name: Acid house: la TB-303 de Chicago
Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit: Neil Rushton y Virgin

refs.q: That’s why at the Haçienda, [DJ] Mike Pickering was playing the Detroit records before anyone in London.
refs.para: While techno struggled for acceptance in London and Belgium in the late 1980s, other English cities began relating to techno and acid house on a more basic level. In particular, the Northern Soul fans in cities like Birmingham, Sheffield, and Manchester seemed to recognize the loose connection Neil Rushton had drawn between Detroit’s Motown past and its electronic future. In no small way, these fans would help connect England’s general interest in soul music to the new electronic dance sounds coming from Detroit, creating a window of opportunity in an environment where techno was still treated as a mere offshoot of Chicago house. Says Rushton, “In the north of England, there had always been a following for soul records, especially from Detroit. That’s why at the Haçienda, [DJ] Mike Pickering was playing the Detroit records before anyone in London. Like me, he’d grown up on this diet of soul music.”

podcast.title: Rise in UK (1990)
podcast.body: The rise of Madchester in the UK in the spring of 1990 contributed to rock's quick resurgence, alongside the beginnings of Grunge in the US. "There was the rise of Madchester in the UK..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: "Holy Trinity" of Bands
podcast.body: The movement's "Holy Trinity" of bands included the Inspiral Carpets (on Mute Records), the Happy Mondays (part of Factory Records), and The Stone Roses (signed to Silver-Tone Records), each offering a distinct yet fresh sound. "The Holy Trinity was the Inspiral Carpets on the roster of mute records, the Happy Mondays, part of factory records, and the Stone Roses who were signed to Silver-Tone Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Scene" as Press Invention
podcast.body: The notion of a distinct "Madchester scene or sound" was largely an invention of the British music press, rather than a self-defined artistic movement, though a sudden interest arose in several new bands from the city. "There wasn't so much of a scene or sound, that was actually the invention of the British music press, but there was a sudden interest in several new bands from Madchester, all of whom recorded for independent labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bridge to Britpop
podcast.body: After a brief lull following Madchester's decline, Britpop emerged, with its foundations essentially built upon the Madchester scene. "then there's a bit of a law and then Brickpop comes along. But Brickpop's foundations were essentially Manchester."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Coining of the Term "Madchester" and "Rave On"
podcast.body: The term "Madchester" originated from two individuals from Newcastle who were creating videos for the Happy Mondays' "Rave On" EP. While searching for a title for tracks about all-night warehouse parties, a band associate (referred to as "Balsaw, the buddy on the album") jokingly suggested "Rave On." The press then reported on a "song about all night parties that they call raves," leading to the widespread adoption of "raves" for these events and "Madchester" for the scene, initially born from a casual remark. "And Balsaw, the buddy on the album, picks a buddy on the album up and went, oh, it's called Rave On. Just for a bit of fun. And then the next day the press was like, oh, this song about all night parties, that the call raves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cultural Hub at The Haçienda
podcast.body: The Haçienda nightclub in Manchester was a focal point for the Madchester scene, with its balconies and stairwells offering a unique vantage point for observing the rise of this genre and the emergence of DJs as prominent figures. "The balconies and stairwells were ringside seats to the explosion in rave music and mad chester in the rise of the DJ as star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Cultural Impact and Travel
podcast.body: During its peak, Madchester clubs were so popular that people would travel extensively from London via coaches and trains, arriving at Piccadilly Station on Fridays and Saturdays to spend the weekend in Manchester. This was unusual for Londoners to travel to "provincial cities." "the first time ever you'd been a club and you'd hear people would come up from London, get a coach... All these Londoners piling off to go, you know, and staying in Manchester for the weekend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Definition and Flourishing Period
podcast.body: Madchester was a crazy and wildly popular music scene that flourished in Manchester, England, in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It was exemplified by bands like the Happy Mondays, Inspiral Carpets, and The Stone Roses, collectively known as the "Holy Trinity." "that crazy and wildly popular scene in Manchester, England that flourished in the late 80s and early 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Duration and Decline
podcast.body: The Madchester era burned brightly and hard for about four years, primarily ending around 1992 or 1993. Its decline was attributed to bands burning out and public interest waning. "the Madchester thing comes to an end somewhere around, what he figured, 92, 93."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Duration and Decline
podcast.body: The Madchester phenomenon "burned very brightly, very hard for about four years," roughly ending around 1992-1993. Its decline was attributed to bands burning out and public interest moving on, leading to a period of lull before the rise of Britpop. "So, Madchester... comes to an end somewhere around what he figured, 92, 93."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence Period (Late 80s - Early 90s)
podcast.body: Madchester refers to a period in the late 1980s and early 1990s when the most exciting new rock music in the UK originated from Manchester, a northern English city. "There was a period in the late 80s and early 90s when the most exciting new rock in the UK was coming out of that northern English city."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Era of Drugs and Debauchery (90s)
podcast.body: The Madchester scene of the 1990s was notoriously associated with extensive drug and alcohol use, characterized by "stories of drugs and alcohol and debauchery," including substances like "Pot Coke, heroin, PCP crack," which led to "wreck brains, wrecked bodies, wrecked cars, wrecked careers." "Now, if you're a fan of the whole madchester thing back in the 90s, you know all about the stories of drugs and alcohol and debauchery."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Fashion Style
podcast.body: The Madchester look was defined by "baggy pants and a bowl haircut," which, despite its retro elements, combined with the music to feel very modern. "Dressed it up with baggy pants and a bowl haircut and you were golden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Foundations
podcast.body: The foundations of Madchester music are rooted in Northern Soul and similar genres. "Madchester's foundations are originally Northern Seoul and stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Golden Period and Decline
podcast.body: Madchester experienced a "golden period" that lasted approximately 18 months before burning out. Factors contributing to its decline included legal hassles for The Stone Roses, drug issues for Happy Mondays, criminal gangs taking over The Haçienda, and Factory Records going out of business. "But madchester's golden period only lasted about 18 months. It just burned out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Holy Trinity
podcast.body: The scene was famously led by a "Holy Trinity" of bands: Inspiral Carpets, Happy Mondays, and The Stone Roses. "one of the bands that formed the Holy Trinity of madchester."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Independent Label Foundation
podcast.body: A defining characteristic of the Madchester movement was that all the new bands gaining attention recorded for independent labels, highlighting the crucial role of the indie world in their development. "all of whom recorded for independent labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Blur
podcast.body: The Madchester movement, along with bands like The Stone Roses, was a foundational influence on Blur's early sound. Blur gradually transitioned from these roots into their distinct Britpop style. "Blur pasó del match, este era poco a poco que me tienes el V-pop."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Influence on British Indie Music
podcast.body: Madchester music set the stage for much of the British indie music that emerged over the subsequent 15 years, with its impact still felt today. "This was music that set the stage for much of the British indie music that was to come for the next 15 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Londoners Traveling to Manchester
podcast.body: During the Madchester era, it became a bizarre phenomenon for people from London to travel by coach or train to Manchester's clubs, particularly on Fridays and Saturdays. This was unusual for Londoners, who typically did not travel to provincial cities for entertainment. "the first time ever you'd been a club, and you'd hear people would come up from London, you'd get a coach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Origin and Era
podcast.body: Madchester was a "crazy and wildly popular scene" that emerged in Manchester, England, flourishing in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It is described as music that "set the stage for much of the British indie music that was to come for the next 15 years," with its impact still felt today. "In 1990, commercial reign for the Inspiral Carpet, one of the bands that formed the Holy Trinity of madchester, that crazy and wildly popular scene in Manchester, England that flourished in the late 80s and early 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Overshadowing Dreampop (1990s)
podcast.body: Madchester is listed as one of the new music genres of the 1990s that began to overshadow Dreampop, contributing to its recession to the margins of popular music.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scene Burnout
podcast.body: The Madchester scene experienced a rapid decline and "burned itself out after a couple of years," particularly influenced by the legal troubles faced by The Stone Roses with their record label. "Manchester burned itself out after a couple of years, especially after the Stone Roses got trapped in what seemed like a bottomless legal quagmire with their record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scene Over by Early 90s
podcast.body: The Madchester scene, featuring bands like The Stone Roses and Happy Mondays, was "pretty much over" by the early 1990s, contributing to a "big void in British music" that Britpop later helped to fill. "The madchester scene featuring the stone roses and the happy Mondays was pretty much over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sound Formation - Late 1980s
podcast.body: The Madchester sound emerged from young Manchester musicians combining the attitude of acid house raves with proper guitars. This resulted in a clash of jangly guitars, swirling organs, and indie rock aesthetics set to a danceable beat, discovered by the British music press by late 1989. "And by late 1989, the British music press had discovered it and were calling the sound madchester."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: UK Resurgence (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Madchester swept through the UK in the early 1990s, following an explosion of dance culture throughout the 1980s, indicating early signs of musical shifts. "Madchester had swept through the UK following an explosion of dance culture through the 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
